summary:
Lesser Poland (Małopolska) stands under Poland's national framework. Criminal law, hate-crime provisions, partnership recognition, entry rules and conditions in custody are set nationally and are carried by the national record. The facts specific to this voivodeship concern its own local-government record.

The voivodeship council adopted an 'LGBT-free' resolution and repealed it on 20 September 2021, after threats to European Commission funding. Council leader Jan Duda, father of president Andrzej Duda, had voted only weeks earlier to keep the resolution in place. The repeal removed a formal declaration of exclusion issued by the regional authority.

In Kraków, the mayor elected in 2024, Aleksander Miszalski, made attendance at the city's annual LGBT Equality March one of his first decisions, becoming the first Kraków mayor to take part after a predecessor declined. He pledged to hang a rainbow flag at city hall and said he wanted 'a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone'.
tangentialFactors:
The voivodeship council and the city of Kraków are separate authorities with different postures. The regional body's declaration was rescinded under external funding pressure, while the capital's mayor has publicly joined the annual equality march and pledged to fly a rainbow flag at city hall.

The repeal followed threats to European Commission funding; the sources do not attribute it to a court ruling or to a change in the voivodeship's competences.
localsOnly:
The 'LGBT-free' resolution was adopted by the voivodeship council, the regional authority, and its repeal in September 2021 removed a formal declaration of exclusion issued by that body. The sources record no change to criminal, civil or family law attached to either the declaration or its repeal.

Kraków's mayor pledged to hang a rainbow flag at city hall, a municipal act rather than a regional one.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not record any region-specific enforcement action, prosecution, hate-crime case or violent incident in Lesser Poland. The council's declaration and its repeal are recorded as political acts, and the sources do not state what legal effect, if any, the declaration had on residents or visitors.

Whether the voivodeship or the city of Kraków has adopted any measure on document markers, facilities access, healthcare provision or partnership recognition is not addressed in these sources.
